question: Which of the following is the MOST important reason an anaesthesiologist establishes central venous access rather than a peripheral IV in a patient with severe septic shock?

answers.text: Central venous access is always faster to insert than peripheral IV

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Peripheral IV insertion is generally faster; central access is preferred here for other reasons.

answers.text: Central venous access allows infusion of vasopressors and high-concentration solutions safely

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Vasopressors and hyperosmolar solutions can cause tissue necrosis if extravasated peripherally; central access allows safe delivery directly into a high-flow vessel.

answers.text: Central venous access avoids the need for strict aseptic technique

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Central venous access actually demands more rigorous aseptic technique (full barrier precautions) compared to peripheral IV insertion.

answers.text: Central venous access is only required for monitoring CVP and is not used for drug infusion

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Central venous catheters are used both for drug infusion (including vasopressors) and CVP monitoring.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the indications for central venous access — focus on why certain drugs and solutions cannot be safely given peripherally.
Well done. Central access is essential when vasopressors or concentrated solutions are required, where peripheral administration poses serious risk.
